"Mom, quit fat talking—I'm trying to eat (mindfully) here!": Evaluating a sociocultural model of family fat talk, positive body image, and mindful eating in college women
Jennifer B. Webba,b,∗ , Courtney B. Rogersb , Lena Etzelb , Meagan P. Padroa
• a UNC Charlotte Department of Psychological Science, United States
• b UNC Charlotte Health Psychology Ph.D. Program, United States
ARTICLE INFO
Keywords: Mindful eating Family fat talk Body appreciation Functional body appreciation Positive body image College women
ABSTRACT

A growing evidence base confirms sociocultural theory's predictions regarding the influence of direct exposure to family factors (e.g., parental commentary) in promoting disordered eating behavior as mediated by negative body image. Nevertheless, this model has not been specifically applied to investigating indirect or vicarious exposure to family communications (e.g., negative body talk) in estimating mindful eating behavior via positive body image intervening variables. Therefore, to address this gap the present study provided a preliminary evaluation of the indirect effects of overhearing family fat talk through both body appreciation and functional body appreciation in predicting mindful eating among undergraduate females. Participants included 333 women attending a large southeastern public university who completed measures of mindful eating, family fat talk, body appreciation, and functional body appreciation via an online survey platform. Results indicated that family fat talk was inversely associated with mindful eating, body appreciation, and functional body appreciation. Whereas engaging in mindful eating positively corresponded with both positive body image indices. A regression model controlling for BMI also revealed that an orientation towards appreciating what the body can do (and not a general appreciation of the body) helped explain the inverse association between family fat talk and mindful eating. Our initial findings tentatively suggest that focusing on the self-objectifying and self-denigrating bodyrelated commentary of family members may disrupt attention to one's own appreciation of the (internal) workings of the body thereby undermining the mindful eating process. Implications for further expanding the translation of sociocultural theory in the context of positive body image and mindful eating are considered.
1. Introduction

Evidence supports the Tripartite Influence Model's (Thompson, Heinberg, Altabe, & Tantleff-Dunn, 1999) predicted relationships between family appearance-related commentary (e.g., weight teasing, critical messages about food choices, etc.) and disordered eating behavior (Rodgers & Chabrol, 2009; Rodgers, 2012). Research further confirms that forms of negative body image indirectly link familial pressures to conform to rigid appearance standards and restrictive eating norms with maladaptive eating patterns with the relationships typically more salient for women and girls (Kluck, 2010; Rodgers, Faure, & Chabrol, 2009a; Rodgers, Paxton, & Chabrol, 2009b). In addition to direct verbal communications about the child's appearance and eating, parents and in particular mothers may also indirectly contribute to creating a heightened appearance-focused family climate through disclosing self-related weight talk (Neumark-Sztainer et al., 2010). Such

appearance-centric verbalizations about one's weight, shape or other aspect of one's physical appearance is reflective of the broader construct of body talk, which may further be categorized into negative, positive, and self-accepting dimensions (Rudiger & Winstead, 2013).

Fat talk is a specific form of negative body talk, which has received considerable attention in the existing literature (see Shannon & Mills, 2015 for a comprehensive review). Fat talk conversations are characterized by vocalizing self-deprecating evaluations of one's own body (e.g., "I look so fat in these jeans.") in the presence of others (Shannon & Mills, 2015). Simultaneously, fat talk may also be understood as a relational manifestation of self-objectification or having internalized an outside observer's perspective in relating to one's body (Fredrickson & Roberts, 1997). Increasingly, research implicates fat talk as a unique contributor to body image distress and is correlated with numerous other adverse consequences, including disordered eating (Shannon & Mills, 2015).

Although most research has examined fat talk within peer relationships (Shannon & Mills, 2015), contemporary scholarship has started exploring this construct as it unfolds within the family environment (Arroyo & Andersen, 2016; Chow & Tan, 2018; Lydecker, Riley, & Grilo, 2018; MacDonald, Dimitropoulos, Royal, Polanco, & Dionne, 2015; Rogers, Martz, Webb, & Galloway, 2017; Romo & Mireles-Rios, 2016). Like restrictive/critical caregiver eating messages (Kroon Van Diest & Tylka, 2010) and negative parental weight-related commentary (Berge, Trofholz, Fong Blue, & Neumark-Sztainer, 2015; Wansink, Latimer, & Pope, 2017), overhearing fat talk transpiring among family members may serve many functions that impact body image and eating behaviors. These may include reinforcing the importance of the thin ideal and reminding women that they are valued largely for their appearance (i.e., body objectification).

In this context, the present study extends previous research grounded in the sociocultural model supporting the specific role of family influences (i.e., parental commentary) on negative body image and maladaptive eating processes in college women in two important ways (Kluck, 2010; Rodgers et al., 2009b,). First, to address the limitations of earlier scholarship which relied on a single-item to measure parental weight talk (Neumark-Sztainer et al., 2010), we selected a recently developed and validated measure of family fat talk which captures a more comprehensive assessment of the construct (MacDonald et al., 2015). Second, research applying the sociocultural model in accounting for variability in the experiences of positive body image and adaptive eating processes are limited (e.g., Augustus-Horvath & Tylka, 2011; Avalos & Tylka, 2006; Tylka & Homan, 2015).

Pursuing this latter aim is responsive to the modern zeitgeist of theory and scholarship guided by the Positive Psychology movement and the integration of Eastern approaches to promoting well-being (e.g., mindfulness) as applied to the domains of eating and body image (Framson et al., 2009; Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a). Indeed, contemporary science confirms the need to bolster efforts to not only focus on mitigating risk for negative body image and disordered eating but to also give increased attention to a complementary focus on stimulating positive forms of embodiment (Piran, 2015). Thus, it is integral to continue to identify sociocultural factors that may predict adaptive forms of embodiment as a first step towards the subsequent development of health promotion programs targeting enhancing positive body image and healthy eating protective factors that may also serve to reduce the risk for the development of negative body image and unhealthy eating practices (Halliwell, 2015; Piran, 2015).

Therefore, the current analysis provides a preliminary evaluation of a partial sociocultural model of mindful eating informed by the Tripartite Influence framework (Rodgers et al., 2009b; Thompson et al., 1999) in a college female sample. This model featured the frequency of overhearing family members engaging in fat talk as the principal contextual influence variable and two measures of positive body image operationalized as body appreciation and functional body appreciation as potential mediators. Mindful eating is an approach to food intake characterized by a nonjudgmental awareness of and response to bodily cues that indicate hunger and satiety (Framson et al., 2009). It is also defined by an intentional focus on food while consuming it (i.e., paying attention to sensory properties and singularly focusing on the act of eating; Framson et al., 2009). A growing body of scholarship supports the numerous health benefits associated with this embodied eating practice (Beshara, Hutchinson, & Wilson, 2013; Framson et al., 2009; Hulbert-Williams, Nicholls, Joy, & Hulbert-Williams, 2014; Hutchinson, Charters, Prichard, Fletcher, & Wilson, 2017; Jordan, Wang, Donatoni, & Meier, 2014).

Body appreciation the more general positive body image concept, reflects holding favorable attitudes towards one's body, taking care of the body via adaptive health behaviors, respecting one's body, and protecting the body by rejecting the narrowly-defined media ideal as the exclusive metric of beauty (Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015b). Whereas for example, functional body appreciation, a more specific

concept is described as being grateful for the body's performance capacities and what it enables the individual to do or experience (Rubin & Steinberg, 2011). Women with positive body image may have grown up in an environment that encourages them to focus on aspects of their body other than appearance (such as what the body can do), which may discourage self-objectification (Frisén & Holmqvist, 2010; Menzel & Levine, 2011).

For instance, increased levels of body appreciation have been linked to lower frequency of negative body talk amongst women (Wasylkiw & Butler, 2014). Wasylkiw and Butler (2014) further found that engaging in more exercise-related talk with friends predicted body appreciation through body-as-process (i.e., valuing body functionality and competence; Franzoi, 1995) variables in young adult women. Meanwhile, Rubin and Steinberg (2011) found that higher levels of functional body appreciation attenuated the association between body surveillance (a measure of self-objectification) and engaging in unhealthy prenatal behaviors in their sample of first-time moms to be.

It is plausible that women who frequently recall noticing family members engaging in self-objectifying fat talk conversations may be less attuned to body functionality and more focused on environmental or other external cues for governing food consumption (Avalos & Tylka, 2006) which is contradictory to the experience of mindful eating. Mindful eating involves a responsiveness to appetitive cues representing sensitivity to the inner workings of the body (i.e., a specific form of body functionality). Therefore, we reasoned that engagement in mindful eating conceptualized as a self-care practice may reflect an appreciation for the body overall and may particularly demonstrate the ability to access an internal body orientation that represents an appreciation for how the body functions.

Drawing upon the aforementioned sociocultural model and emerging evidence base, we hypothesized that more frequent exposure to family fat talk would be inversely associated with mindful eating, body appreciation, and functional body appreciation in our college female sample. Meanwhile, higher levels of mindful eating were expected to correspond with higher levels of positive body image. We additionally anticipated significant indirect effects of family fat talk on mindful eating via both positive body image variables controlling for BMI would emerge.
2. Method
2.1. Participants

The study sample comprised 3621 undergraduate females from a large publicly-funded institution located in the Southeastern United States. The mean age was 19.4 years (SD = 1.5) and the sample was predominantly White/European American (62%) and Black/African American (21%). The remainder of participants identified as Asian or Asian American (4%), Hispanic or Latina (6%), American Indian/ Alaska Native (< 1%), Multi-ethnic/racial (6%), and Other (1%). The majority of the sample consisted of freshman and sophomore students (76.5%) and 86.5% of the sample were non-psychology majors. The participants had an average body mass index (BMI) of 23.5 kg/m2 (SD = 4.9; "normal weight" range) with 26.8% of the sample classifying as higher weight with a BMI ≥ 25 kg/m2 (i.e., "overweight" and "obese").
2.2. Measures
2.2.1. Demographics
A demographic measure was administered to gather the following

variables: age, race/ethnicity, gender, academic class status, psychology major status, and self-reported weight and height which were used to calculate BMI.
2.2.2. Family fat talk

The 16-item, 2-factor Family Fat Talk Questionnaire (FFTQ-F; MacDonald et al., 2015) measures self-critical, body-related conversations within the family context. Eight items constitute the Family subscale and examine fat talk exhibited by the respondent's family including criticism regarding their physical appearance, such as "When I'm with my family members, I hear them complain that they are fat". The other 8 items (Self subscale) reflect the respondent's engagement in disparaging comments related to his/her body when surrounded by family members (e.g., "When I'm with my family, I complain that I'm not in shape"). All items were rated on a 5-point Likert scale, from 1 (Never) to 5 (Always) with higher scores reflecting higher levels of overhearing or communicating fat talk in the family context. Previous validation work has demonstrated excellent internal consistency of both subscales (Cronbach's alpha of Self, α = 0.88; Family, α = 0.90; MacDonald et al., 2015). In terms of convergent validity, both subscales significantly correlated with peer fat talk, body dissatisfaction (which mirrors the content of fat talk conversations), and social physique anxiety. A modest correlation between the two subscales (r = 0.34, p = .002; MacDonald et al., 2015) supported the related, yet independent nature of the constructs. Temporal stability of the FFTQ scores was shown to be present across two weeks (MacDonald et al., 2015). The present analysis only focused on the Family subscale, which demonstrated an excellent level of internal consistency (α = 0.92).
2.2.3. Body appreciation

The 10-item Body Appreciation Scale-2 (BAS-2; Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015b) was used to assess respondent's acceptance of and respect for their own bodies. This revised measure contains five original items of the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS; Avalos, Tylka, & Wood-Barcalow, 2005) and the addition of five adapted or newly developed items that ensure the elimination of sex-specific items as well as the avoidance of language that may be biased towards able-bodied individuals. Using a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (Never) to 5 (Always), participants indicated the extent to which they favor their body (e.g., "I feel good about my body"), even when exposed to mediapromoted appearance ideals, "I feel like I am beautiful even if I am different from media image of attractive people". Higher scores indicate higher levels of body appreciation. Confirmatory factor analyses conducted by Tylka and Wood-Barcalow (2015b) have supported the measure's unidimensionality and invariance across both sex and different sample sources (undergraduate students, and community adults). Cronbach's coefficient alphas of .97 and .96 for both, women and men, respectively, indicated high internal consistency reliability. Further reliability indices suggest a 3-week stability of BAS-2's scores. A strong positive correlation with appearance evaluation and a significant inverse correlation with body dissatisfaction, body surveillance and internalization of media appearance ideals were found, thus upholding the BAS-2's construct validity (Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015b). Internal consistency in the present sample was excellent (α = .96).
2.2.4. Functional body appreciation

The Functional Body Appreciation Scale (FBApS; Rubin & Steinberg, 2011) is one of two domains of an 11-item measure of body functionality that was developed through qualitative interviews with first-time pregnant women (see Rubin, 2006 for further details regarding scale construction). Five items were used to measure participant's appreciation of their body's capabilities (e.g., "I have been grateful for what my body has allowed me to do"). Responses were rated using a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 5 (Strongly Agree) and higher scores indicated greater appreciation of body functionality. Cronbach's alpha coefficient was 0.82 in the original validation sample

(Rubin & Steinberg, 2011). In terms of further validity indices, correlational analyses revealed a significant negative association with body surveillance, depressive symptoms and engagement in less healthy prenatal behaviors (Rubin & Steinberg, 2011). Internal consistency in the present study was acceptable (α = 0.70).
2.2.5. Mindful eating

The 28-item Mindful Eating Questionnaire (MEQ; Framson et al., 2009) consists of five subscales to assess one's orientation towards food intake along with the awareness of related sensory properties. The disinhibition subscale examines the extent to which participants are attuned to their internal hunger and satiety cues, using items such as "I stop eating when I'm full even when eating something I love". An example item of the second subscale is "I taste every bite of food that I eat" and captures participant's awareness of sensory experiences, including appearance and flavor of foods. Being able to resist external food consumption cues was assessed via items such as "I recognize when food advertisements make me want to eat" and the fourth subscale tapped into eating as an emotional response, (e.g., "When I'm sad I eat to feel better"). The distraction subscale measured participant's cognitive preoccupation while eating. The full-scale score was the focus of the present analysis. All items were rated on a 4-point Likert scale ranging from 1 = Never to 4 = Always, with a higher mean score indicating a higher overall mindful eating orientation. Psychometric properties indicated adequate internal consistency reliability of the MEQ summary score (α =0.64; Framson et al., 2009). In support of the construct validity of the scale, the MEQ was negatively correlated with BMI and independent from cognitive restraint (Framson et al., 2009). In line with the expected emphasis on mindfulness, Framson et al. (2009) demonstrated the scale's positive correlation with engagement in regular yoga practice. Cronbach's alpha for the full scale in the present sample was strong (α = 0.84).
2.3. Procedure

Subsequent to receiving IRB approval, participants were recruited through the Department of Psychology's online research sign-up system. Following provision of passive consent, participants completed the set of measures in a randomized sequence to minimize order effects using the Qualtrics survey administration platform. As an incentive, students received research credit in a participating psychology course.
2.4. Data analyses

The data analyses were carried out in four stages. First, we inspected the data to evaluate the amount of missingness at the variable level and determined whether a systematic pattern occurred. Second, basic descriptive statistics were conducted to assess whether the distributional characteristics of the data met assumptions of normality. Third, to address the first hypothesis, basic correlations were computed to establish the linear associations between the key study variables. Lastly, Hayes' (2013) PROCESS macro model 4 for SPSS was used to detect the potential predicted indirect effects using multiple regression of the zscores for each variable in a combined model adjusted for BMI. This non-parametric method is based on a bootstrap resampling technique and yields an indirect effect beta coefficient estimate alongside a biascorrected 95% confidence interval (CI). Statistical significance is demonstrated when the 95% CI excludes zero. Ten thousand random resamples with replacement were performed for the multiple indirect model. This robust analytic approach is now considered the strategy of choice over the traditional Baron and Kenny (1986) causal steps test of mediation and the corresponding Sobel test (Sobel, 1982) for more directly evaluating the magnitude and significance of an indirect effect (Preacher & Hayes, 2008).

3. Results
3.1. Preliminary analyses

Inspection of the magnitude of missing data at the variable level indicated the following percentages: BMI (6.1%), MEQ (5%), FFTQ-F (5.8%), BAS-2 (4.4%), and FBApS (5.2%). Despite these non-negligible amounts (see Parent, 2013 for a discussion), listwise deletion was used as the approach for handling missing data in the present analysis. Implementing a complete case analysis is supported in instances such as ours in which there is evidence of no systematic pattern in the missing data (i.e., missing completely at random; MCAR; Little's Test: X2 (31) = 20.37, p = .93) and when there is minimal risk of data removal compromising achieving adequate power to detect significant effects (Allison, 2014; Grace-Martin, n.d.). For example, according to expert guidelines (Fritz & MacKinnon, 2007), the analytic sample size of 333 far exceeds the required minimum N of 148 to observe an indirect effect comprising a small to medium-sized alpha pathway coefficient (i.e., from predictor to proposed mediator) and a small to medium-sized beta pathway coefficient (i.e., from proposed mediator to criterion) at 80% power using bias-corrected bootstrapping estimating procedures.

Examination of the distributional qualities of the primary study variables failed to reveal significant departures from normality with regard to skewness (< 3.0) or kurtosis (< 10.0). Therefore, given that these parameters fell within the acceptable ranges as outlined by Kline (2010), no additional data transformations beyond the creation of zscores were performed. Z-scores were generated in order to enhance the interpretation of the regression coefficients across measurement instruments. Table 1 presents the means, standard deviations, and correlations for the key study variables. All of the linear associations observed were in the predicted directions. For instance, as hypothesized family fat talk was negatively correlated with body appreciation, functional body appreciation, and mindful eating. Meanwhile, mindful eating was positively associated with both measures of positive body image. Possessing a higher BMI corresponded with reporting higher levels of family fat talk and lower levels of mindful eating and positive body image.
3.2. Multiple indirect effect model analysis

A graphical representation of the results obtained from the multiple indirect effect model featuring standardized beta weights is found in Fig. 1. This concurrent model enabled isolating the unique effects of each potential positive body image mediating variable while simultaneously adjusting for the contributions of the other thereby also reducing Type 1 error inflation. Screening of multicollinearity diagnostic parameters failed to detect significant concerns with the inclusion of variables with overlapping variance structures in the model as both tolerance (> 0.20) and variance inflation factor (< 10) indices were within the acceptable ranges.

The full model accounted for 20% of the variance in mindful eating scores (BMI: β = −0.01, p = .87, 95% CI: −0.11 to 0.09; FFTQ-F: β = −0.09, p = .09, 95% CI: −0.19 to 0.01; BAS-2: β = 0.10, p = .13, 95% CI: −0.03 to 0.23; FBApS: β = 0.35, p < .001, 95% CI: 0.22 to 0.47). Analyses controlling for BMI produced a significant total effect

This estimate reflects an indirect effect composed of a small alpha pathway and a small to medium-sized beta pathway (Fritz & MacKinnon, 2007). 4. Discussion

The present study provided a preliminary evaluation of a sociocultural model of mindful eating grounded in the larger Tripartite Influence Model (Thompson et al., 1999) and supported by research illuminating the specific role of family factors (e.g., parental commentary) in this theoretical framework (e.g., Kluck, 2010; Rodgers et al., 2009a; Rodgers et al., 2009b). Specifically, we assessed whether the frequency of overhearing family members complaining about their own physical appearance (i.e., fat talk) negatively predicted mindful eating through two closely-related positive body image variables. Results were mostly in the hypothesized directions.

As predicted, overhearing family participate in self-denigrating body commentary was inversely associated with mindful eating, general body appreciation, and specifically appreciating the body's functionality. Additionally, more frequent mindful eating corresponded with higher levels of both positive body image indices. Collectively, these findings extend previous research showing negative or appearance-focused body talk's positive link to disordered eating (see Shannon & Mills, 2015 for a review) and negative association with body appreciation (Wasylkiw & Butler, 2014). Findings also build upon earlier scholarship which has exclusively focused on examining the relationships of family fat talk with dimensions of negative body image and dysfunctional eating behavior (MacDonald et al., 2015) and the association of mindful eating with body image disturbances (Alberts & Raes, 2012; Hulbert-Williams et al., 2014).

We also found partial support for our initial test of the sociocultural model in predicting mindful eating in the current sample. When considered in concert, only an appreciation for the body's functionality (or body-as-process; Franzoi, 1995) emerged as a significant (albeit modest in size) explanatory mechanism in the link between family fat talk disclosures and overall mindful eating behavior. This finding highlights the potential unique risk of exposure to a family climate inundated with negative, self-objectifying body talk in undermining mindful eating processes specifically as a result of compromised appreciation for the functional properties of the body, beyond holding a more generalized positive stance towards the body. This result makes sense if we understand mindful eating to be an approach to food consumption that accentuates an embodied connection to the inner workings of how the body functions, particularly with respect to enhancing attunement with and responsiveness to internal hunger and satiety cues (Framson et al., 2009). However, due to the rather small effect size it will be critical to replicate this finding in other samples in order to strengthen the reliability of these claims.

Overall, our preliminary findings extend earlier tests of family-related influences such as direct parental commentary stemming from sociocultural theory (Thompson et al., 1999) in predicting negative body image and disordered eating (e.g., Kluck, 2010; Rodgers et al., 2009a; Rodgers et al., 2009b). We demonstrated that this model featuring the indirect influence of overhearing family fat talk can be successfully applied to accounting for variability in positive body image and mindful eating in a college female sample. These results may have implications for expanding the sociocultural model's future application

4.1. Strengths, limitations, and future research directions

The present study provides an incremental contribution to the mindful eating, fat talk, and positive body image literature. It uniquely offers a preliminary understanding of why overhearing family members engage in fat talk negatively predicts mindful eating grounded in positive body image-related variables that prioritize engaging an internal body orientation and eschewing a self-objectifying, external appearance-driven stance. Nevertheless, the current findings must be interpreted within the context of the following caveats, which provide additional avenues for future research to consider pursuing.

First, the current analysis exclusively focused on the experiences of college women who primarily identified as White or European American. Therefore, it would be advantageous to attempt to replicate the findings among larger samples of ethnic minority college women, undergraduate men as well as among women and men in the community. Although a significant indirect effect did emerge in our combined model we did not test for true mediation (Maxwell & Cole, 2007) and therefore causality should not be inferred. We encourage subsequent researchers to test the tenability of our model in experimental paradigms or longitudinal designs.

The effect size for functional body appreciation in our concurrent indirect effect model was relatively small though statistically significant. It is possible that two factors could have contributed to mitigating this observed effect. First, our study relied on a measure of negative body talk occurring in the family environment. It is plausible that if we included a measure of overhearing positive/self-accepting body talk (e.g., Greer, Campione-Barr, & Lindell, 2014; Hart, Chow, & Tan, 2017; Romo & Mireles-Rios, 2016; Rudiger & Winstead, 2013) or of functionality/exercise-related body talk (e.g., Wasylkiw & Butler, 2014) being communicated in the family, these variables may have evidenced stronger associations with the measures of positive body image and mindful eating featured. Second, our participants consisted of a nonclinical sample of young adult women. It is likely that larger effects would have been produced by targeting a clinical sample of women with higher exposures to family fat talk, elevated body image disturbance and/or with an eating disorder.

Moreover, we did not assess how frequently our participants have contact with their family members on a regular basis. It is possible that young women who are still living at home attending college or who frequently communicate via the phone versus those who do not may
have greater exposure to overhearing family fat talk. Future research should further clarify the relevance of this factor.

Additionally, as this was a partial test of the sociocultural model (Rodgers et al., 2009b; Thompson et al., 1999) it would also be important for later studies to include measures of internalization of beauty ideals and appearance comparison processes to provide a fuller evaluation of this theoretical framework in this particular context. The present indirect effect model could also be further expanded to assess inclusion of established measures of self-objectification and other relational characteristics (e.g., family food talk, perceived body acceptance by others, etc.) alongside novel measures of functionality comparison (Mulgrew & Tiggemann, 2016) in contributing incremental explanatory power.

Finally, two measurement limitations in the present investigation are worth further consideration. Indeed, the measure used to quantify family fat talk in the current study does not permit clarifying which family member or members the participant recalls engaging in this type of negative body commentary. It is possible that overhearing one's mom versus one's dad or a sibling (of the same or different gender) could yield differential effects. Therefore, we recommend future research providing a more fine-tuned analysis of the potential impact of various sources of family fat talk in this context. Also, although the instrument used to assess functional body appreciation reached an acceptable threshold of internal consistency, it was originally developed and validated in a community sample of pregnant women (Rubin & Steinberg, 2011). It is likely that this unique developmental transition for women stimulates heightened awareness of and appreciation for what the body is able to do. Thus, body functionality in certain respects is presumably more salient in this select female sample than perhaps among college women in general. Therefore, scientists are encouraged to consider using a newly-developed and validated measure of functionality appreciation that may be applicable across a more diverse range of participant characteristics (e.g., gender, age, ability, etc.; Alleva, Tylka, & Kroon Van Diest, 2017).
5. Conclusions

The present study provided a novel preliminary partial test of sociocultural theory as applied to mindful eating in college women. Results suggest that limited appreciation of the functional qualities of the body helps explain why vicarious exposure to family members' selfobjectifying body talk exerts a negative influence on mindful eating behavior.
